blocks.text: **The problem.** Design a class `KthLargest` that finds the **kth largest** value in a stream of numbers. The constructor `KthLargest(k, nums)` receives `k` and the first values. Each call to `add(val)` adds a value to the stream and returns the kth largest value so far. (The kth largest means in sorted order — duplicates count — and there are always at least k values when you're asked.)

blocks.alt: A stream of numbers. The class keeps only the 3 largest values seen so far, 4, 5 and 8, in a min-heap. Its top, 4, the smallest of the three largest, is the 3rd largest value of the whole stream.

elements.text: the 3 largest so far, in a min-heap
elements.originalText: the 3 largest so far, in a min-heap

blocks.code:
KthLargest(3, [4, 5, 8, 2])
add(3)  -> 4      the values are 2 3 4 5 8: the 3rd largest is 4
add(5)  -> 5      2 3 4 5 5 8
add(10) -> 5      2 3 4 5 5 8 10
add(9)  -> 8      2 3 4 5 5 8 9 10
add(4)  -> 8

blocks.text: 1. Brute force: sort everything on every add
**add: O(n log n) time; space O(n)**, where n is the number of values so far — and it keeps growing.
Sort once in the constructor. Then each new value only needs to be **inserted in its place**: binary search finds the spot in O(log n), and the kth largest sits at a fixed distance from the end.
**add: O(n) time; space O(n).** Better, but every value ever added is still kept — and still shifted.
The key idea: only the k largest matter

A value that has already been pushed out of the top k can **never** be the kth largest again — the stream only adds values, so it only gets pushed further down. So keep just the **k largest**, in a **min-heap**. Its top is the smallest of them: exactly the kth largest. When a new value arrives, push it; if the heap now holds k + 1 values, pop the smallest — it just fell out of the top k.

blocks.alt: The adds from the example with k = 3. Starting from the heap 4, 5, 8: add 3 drops 3 and returns 4. Add 5 drops 4 and returns 5. Add 10 drops 5 and returns 5. Add 9 drops 5 and returns 8. Add 4 drops 4 and returns 8. The heap never holds more than 4 values.
blocks.caption: Green: the top of the heap — the answer to each add.

blocks.text: 3. Best solution: a min-heap of size k

blocks.caption: The heap never holds more than k + 1 values; its top is always the answer.

blocks.text: **add: O(log k) time; space O(k).** The constructor costs O(n log k). Memory no longer grows with the stream — only with k.

rows.approach: Brute force: sort everything on every add
rows.timeWhy: Every `add` **re-sorts** all n values so far.
rows.spaceWhy: Every value ever added, and it **keeps growing**.

rows.timeWhy: Binary search finds the spot in log n, but **inserting shifts** the values after it.

rows.approach: Best: a min-heap of size k
rows.timeWhy: Each `add` is **one push** and maybe one pop on a heap of **k**.

items: **Fewer than k values at the start** — `KthLargest(3, [5])`: the heap simply holds fewer than k values until enough arrive. (The problem promises there are k values whenever `add` is asked for an answer.)
**k = 1** — the heap holds one value: the maximum so far.
**Duplicates** — `add(5)` twice counts twice: `[5, 5, 8]` has 5 as both the 2nd and 3rd largest.
**Small values arriving late** — once the heap is full, a value smaller than its top goes in and comes straight back out.
**Kth Largest Element in an Array** — the same heap over a fixed array. Two lessons ahead.
**The k largest values themselves** — return the heap's contents instead of its top.
**Kth smallest in a stream** — flip it: a **max**-heap of the k smallest.
**Find Median from Data Stream** — a running middle needs **two** heaps. The last lesson.
